title: A Pulsed Live-Cell Quantum Microscope for Entangled Solid State and Biological Qubits
authors: Javier Noé Ramos-Silva, Sangjun Noh, Minghao Jiang, Parisa Aghaei, Ayla Hazrathosseini, Jocelyn Leon, Philip Hemmer, Peter J. Burke
abstract: Two revolutions in quantum sensing are converging on the same microscope stage. Biological qubits have emerged as genetically encoded, optically addressable quantum systems inside live cells. Solid state spin based qubits have been entangled and used as nanoscale correlator magnetometers, delivering sensitivity and spatial-resolution gains that single-spin probes cannot reach. Here we report a pulsed quantum microscope that enables simultaneous quantum state manipulation of both qubit technologies in live cells. The platform combines nanosecond-gated optical excitation at 450 nm and 520 nm, three-dimensional diffraction-limited addressing by galvo beam scanning and piezo objective focus, rapidly switched static and radio-frequency magnetic fields, single-photon timing with picosecond resolution, and microwave control for frequencies from DC to 5 GHz, including the 2.87 GHz resonance of solid state spins, the 500 MHz to 800 MHz resonance of radical pairs in biological qubits, and any future qubit resonance in the GHz range. Live cell imaging with simultaneous biological and solid state nanoparticle qubits in the same cell demonstrates the power of this technique for multiplexed quantum sensing. We anticipate this approach will open new opportunities for researchers to explore quantum sensing in live cells, and, ultimately, entanglement between a solid-state qubit and a protein-hosted spin qubit.
summary: The paper introduces a revolutionary pulsed quantum microscope designed to simultaneously probe and manipulate both solid-state NV center qubits and genetically encoded biological spin qubits inside living cells. By integrating advanced optics, fast pulsing electronics, and multi-frequency control, the platform enables multiplexed quantum sensing. This breakthrough paves the way for realizing entanglement between artificial solid-state systems and complex biological quantum states.
main_problem: The central challenge is developing a single, integrated quantum microscope capable of simultaneously manipulating and sensing both solid-state (NV center) and genetically encoded biological qubits within the complex environment of live cells.
main_result: The authors report the development of a pulsed quantum microscope platform that successfully integrates dual excitation paths, time-resolved detection, and microwave control to enable multiplexed quantum sensing in living systems.
method: The methodology involves building an advanced optical setup on an inverted microscope body, combining nanosecond-gated pulsing with precise magnetic field control across multiple frequency ranges (DC to 5 GHz).
model_or_system: The platform integrates solid-state qubits (NV centers in diamond) and biological spin qubits (e.g., MagLOV/flavin radical pairs). The system is designed for pulsed operation, allowing time-resolved measurements on both types of qubits simultaneously.
key_observables: Quantum state manipulation, single-photon timing resolution, NV ODMR signals ($\sim2.87$ GHz), and optically activated delayed fluorescence from biological targets.
important_parameters: Nanosecond pulse gating, picosecond timing resolution, microwave control up to 5 GHz, and the ability to operate in a stationary-sample, live-cell geometry.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that combining these disparate measurement modalities onto one platform overcomes current limitations in quantum sensing for biological applications.
figures_summary: Figures detail the system architecture, showing nested 4f relays, dual excitation paths (520 nm and 450 nm), and schematics of pulsed laser drivers and microwave delivery systems.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by detailing the necessary components—pulsed optics, advanced scanning mechanisms, and frequency control electronics—to merge two previously separate quantum sensing modalities into one unified, live-cell compatible instrument.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it pushes the experimental boundary of open quantum systems by creating a novel interface for controlling entanglement between solid-state defects and chemically sensitive biological molecules in real time.

FIG. 2: Schematic of the pulsed quantum microscope platform. The optical path comprises a fiber-coupled 520 nm laser, four nested 4 f relay systems, a galvo-galvo beam scanner, a confocal pinhole, and a single-photon detector (SPD). The microwave delivery routes a nanosecond-gated signal from the RF generator through a power amplifier and PCB loop antenna positioned beneath the sample. Data acquisition is synchronized with both the optical and microwave channels.

FIG. 3: Dual-excitation configuration at the laser input. A dichroic mirror combines the fiber-coupled 520 nm (NV) and 450 nm (MagLOV) excitation beams into a single collinear path routed through the shared 4f relay, galvo-galvo scanner, and microscope objective.

NV sensing of materials.note: The core capability of the new paper is using NV centers to probe quantum states within a complex environment (live cells), directly aligning with the theme of using spin-defect impurities for advanced sensing applications.
